title: FAQ — Privacy & Data: Why doesn't the website show customer testimonials?
text: Q: Why doesn't the website show customer testimonials? Building that list just to gather testimonials would work against the same no-account, no-tracking design the app is built on, so we've chosen not to. Our App Store and Google Play ratings — left voluntarily, by people we've never contacted — are the closest thing we have to third-party proof.

If it's in the report, it was captured in the field.

title: FAQ — Features & Capture: What types of media can I capture?

title: FAQ — Features & Capture: What metadata is captured automatically?
text: Q: What metadata is captured automatically? A: Every capture is automatically stamped with date, time, and GPS coordinates. Unlike most apps, this metadata stays embedded in your data even when you export or share it — so your proof of time and location travels with the record.

title: FAQ — Features & Capture: Does it work without an internet connection?
text: Q: Does it work without an internet connection? A: Absolutely. Preserver works completely offline — no Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, or mobile data required. GPS capture works via satellite with no network connection at all. Your captures are stored on your device until you choose to back them up or share them.

title: FAQ — Features & Capture: Does GPS work without mobile signal?
text: Q: Does GPS work without mobile signal? A: Yes. GPS positioning uses satellites, not mobile towers or Wi-Fi. It works underground, in aircraft, in remote areas, and anywhere else there is no mobile or data signal. This is one of Preserver's most important features for field users.

title: FAQ — Features & Capture: What is an Activity?
text: Q: What is an Activity? A: An Activity is a container for a related set of captures — for example, a job site visit, a field research session, or a day's notes. Within each Activity you can mix text, voice, photos and video, all sharing the same timestamp and location context.

title: FAQ — Features & Capture: How do I export or share my captures?
text: Q: How do I export or share my captures? A: From within any Activity, you can share directly to other apps, export to your cloud storage, or send via email or messaging. You control exactly what gets shared and with whom. The GPS and timestamp metadata travels with the export.

title: FAQ — Features & Capture: Can I add notes after the fact?
text: Q: Can I add notes after the fact? A: Yes, you can add additional captures to an Activity at any time. The original captures retain their original timestamps, so the record of when each item was captured is always accurate and tamper-evident.

title: FAQ — AI & Transcription: Does Preserver send my audio to any AI service?
text: Q: Does Preserver send my audio to any AI service? A: No. Preserver never uploads your recordings anywhere. These features use the AI already built into your phone by Apple or Google. You choose when and whether to share a file with it.

title: FAQ — AI & Transcription: Does this work offline?
text: Q: Does this work offline? A: Recording and exporting in Preserver always work offline. Apple Intelligence transcription and Notes summaries run on-device. Gemini generally requires an internet connection; Pixel Recorder transcription runs on-device.

title: FAQ — AI & Transcription: Is my exported recording still valid as evidence after transcription?
text: Q: Is my exported recording still valid as evidence after transcription? A: Your original recording in Preserver is untouched — transcription and summarisation work on the exported copy. Keep the original in Preserver (or your export bundle, which includes the timestamped metadata) as your source of record.

title: FAQ — AI & Transcription: What languages are supported?
text: Q: What languages are supported? A: Transcription language support depends on your phone's speech recognition, not on Preserver. Check your device's language settings — on iPhone under Settings → General → Language & Region, and on Android under your speech/voice input settings.

title: FAQ — AI & Transcription: Which phones support this?
text: Q: Which phones support this? A: Apple Intelligence requires iPhone 15 Pro or later running a current version of iOS. Gemini is available on most recent Android phones; on-device summarisation features vary by model. Older phones can still transcribe using Notes (iPhone) or share the file to any transcription app of your choice.

title: FAQ — AI & Transcription: Do I need to pay for anything?

title: FAQ — Platforms & Compatibility: What iOS and Android versions are supported?

title: FAQ — Platforms & Compatibility: Can I use Preserver on multiple devices?
text: Q: Can I use Preserver on multiple devices? A: Yes. Because there's no account, each device operates independently. If you back up to a shared cloud account (e.g., family Google Drive), captures from multiple devices can be stored together. Direct cross-device sync is on our roadmap.

text: Q: Can I use Preserver for professional or compliance purposes? A: Yes. Preserver is used across 40+ industries for timestamped evidence, field records, compliance documentation, and more. title: FAQ — Professional & Compliance Use: Is the timestamp tamper-proof?
text: Q: Is the timestamp tamper-proof? A: The timestamp is captured at the device level at the moment of recording and is not editable within the app. While no digital timestamp is fully tamper-proof in an absolute legal sense, the metadata is embedded and travels with the file, making alterations detectable. For critical legal matters, consult a legal professional.

title: FAQ — Professional & Compliance Use: Can Preserver be used as legal evidence?
text: Q: Can Preserver be used as legal evidence? A: Preserver captures are increasingly used to support legal matters — disputes, insurance claims, workplace incidents and more. Whether records are accepted as evidence depends on the jurisdiction and the context. The GPS and timestamp metadata significantly strengthens the credibility of any capture. Consult a legal professional for your specific situation.

title: When Any Photo Can Be Called Fake, Proof Needs Receipts — Preserver Blog
text: ← All articles Trust & Evidence By Monte Huebsch, Founder September 2026 5 min read When Any Photo Can Be Called Fake, Proof Needs Receipts AI image generation got good enough this year that a new problem showed up in court: people now argue that real evidence is fake. It's called the liar's dividend, and it changes what "proof" needs to look like. For most of photography's history, a photo was treated as proof almost by default. If you had the picture, you had the evidence. That assumption is breaking down — not because fake photos are new, but because anyone can now plausibly claim a real photo is fake. The liar's dividend Researchers have a name for this: the liar's dividend . As deepfakes and AI-generated images become common knowledge, people gain a new defence against real evidence — simply claim it was fabricated. It's already shown up in real cases.

title: When Any Photo Can Be Called Fake, Proof Needs Receipts — Preserver Blog
text: Tesla's legal team argued that past public statements about self-driving safety couldn't be used against the company because they might be deepfakes. A defendant in a Capitol riot case argued the video evidence against him could be AI-generated. Neither claim needed to be true to be useful — raising the doubt was often enough. Why this matters beyond the courtroom You don't need a lawsuit for this to bite. Consider a few everyday situations: A tradesperson's before/after photos get challenged in a customer dispute — "how do I know that's actually from my property, on that day?" An insurance claim photo gets questioned by an adjuster looking for any reason to delay or deny. A workplace incident report gets picked apart during an investigation, with the photographic evidence itself becoming the point of dispute.

title: When Any Photo Can Be Called Fake, Proof Needs Receipts — Preserver Blog
text: In each case, the person relying on the photo now has to answer a question that never used to come up: how do we know this is real? What actually answers that question A photo alone doesn't answer it — not anymore. What does is the data around the photo, captured at the same moment, that can't be edited after the fact: exactly when it was taken, exactly where, and a way to prove the file hasn't been altered since. That's a timestamp, a GPS coordinate, and an integrity hash — not glamorous, but it's the difference between "trust me" and "check for yourself." What Preserver does about it Every capture in Preserver — photo, video, voice note or text — is stamped with time, date and GPS the instant it's recorded, and protected with a SHA-256 integrity hash. None of that is editable after the fact.

title: When Any Photo Can Be Called Fake, Proof Needs Receipts — Preserver Blog
text: It doesn't make a fake image real, and it doesn't stop someone from claiming your photo is fake — but it gives you something to point to besides your word. The best evidence is the kind that doesn't need you to vouch for it. The timestamp and hash speak for themselves. The short version Anyone can generate a convincing fake photo now, and anyone can claim a real one is fake. The way through that isn't a better photo — it's proof that travels with it. title: Getting AI Summaries and Transcripts from Your Preserver Recordings — Preserver Blog
text: ← All articles Features By Monte Huebsch, Founder August 2026 4 min read Getting AI Summaries and Transcripts from Your Preserver Recordings Preserver never uploads or processes your captures with AI — but your phone already has that built in. Here's how to turn a voice or video recording into a transcript or summary, and what to keep in mind if that recording might matter as evidence later. Preserver's job is capture: instant, timestamped, GPS-tagged, and private by default. It doesn't transcribe, summarise, or send anything to a server — there isn't one. But once you've captured a voice note or video, you may still want a written transcript or a quick summary. For that, you don't need a new app. Your phone almost certainly already has one built in.

title: Getting AI Summaries and Transcripts from Your Preserver Recordings — Preserver Blog
text: Your phone already has AI for this On iPhone 15 Pro or later, Apple Intelligence powers transcription and summarisation directly inside the Notes app. On Android, Gemini and the Pixel Recorder app offer the same thing. Both work on recordings from any source — including the ones you've captured in Preserver. Open the Activity in Preserver and use the share sheet to export the voice or video capture Share it to Notes (iPhone) or Gemini / Recorder (Android) Let the built-in AI generate a transcript, and a summary if you want one Save or copy the result wherever you need it — a report, an email, a case file What works offline and what doesn't Recording and exporting in Preserver always work offline — that hasn't changed. Once you hand the file to your phone's AI, it depends on the tool: Apple Intelligence transcription and Notes summaries run entirely on-device, so no connection is needed.

title: Getting AI Summaries and Transcripts from Your Preserver Recordings — Preserver Blog
text: Pixel Recorder transcription is also on-device. Gemini, on the other hand, generally needs an internet connection to process the file. If you're working somewhere without signal, transcribe later once you're back in range — the original capture and its metadata aren't going anywhere. Keep the original as your record A transcript or summary is a convenience layer, not a replacement for the original. Preserver's export bundle carries the embedded timestamp and GPS metadata that makes a capture credible; a transcript generated afterward doesn't inherit that automatically. title: The Network Goes Down More Than You'd Think — Preserver Blog
text: ← All articles Offline By Monte Huebsch, Founder September 2026 4 min read The Network Goes Down More Than You'd Think You don't need to be off-grid for "no signal" to become a problem. In 2026, major cloud and telecom outages have become a weekly occurrence — and most field apps have no answer for it. It's not just you It's easy to assume a dropped connection is a local problem — bad reception, an overloaded tower, a building with thick walls. Often it isn't. Internet monitoring firm ThousandEyes tracked global outage activity through 2026 and found public cloud network outages spiking as much as 72–98% week-on-week at points during the year. Named incidents hit major providers directly: AT&T had three separate outages in September alone; Salesforce had a 4.5-hour outage the same month; Microsoft, Cogent, Cox and Charter all had their own disruptions across the year.

title: The Network Goes Down More Than You'd Think — Preserver Blog
text: These aren't obscure providers — they're the infrastructure most cloud-dependent apps quietly rely on. What breaks when the cloud does Most field-capture and note-taking apps assume the network is there. They sync as you go, save to the cloud by default, or need a live connection to even open. When the network — or the app's own backend — goes down, so does your ability to document anything, right when you might need to most: mid-inspection, mid-job, mid-incident. Offline isn't just for remote work The obvious cases are the ones already covered elsewhere — underground, in aircraft, on rural properties with no towers nearby. But the outages above didn't happen in remote areas. They happened to ordinary cloud services millions of people use every day, in cities, during business hours. Offline-first isn't just a feature for people working off-grid.

If your ability to capture a record depends on someone else's infrastructure staying up, it isn't really your record yet. The short version Network outages aren't a remote-work edge case anymore — they're a regular event at some of the biggest providers online. title: Voice Notes vs Typed Notes: When to Use Each — Preserver Blog
text: ← All articles Features By Monte Huebsch, Founder April 2026 3 min read Voice Notes vs Typed Notes: When to Use Each Both are GPS-tagged and timestamped in Preserver, but voice and text serve different capture situations. Here's a practical guide to choosing the right one on the job. Preserver supports four capture types: text, voice, photo, and video. All four get the same automatic timestamp and GPS tag. But when it comes to day-to-day capture, most people find themselves reaching for either their keyboard or the microphone — and the choice usually comes down to situation, not preference. When voice notes win Voice recording is faster when your hands are occupied. A tradie on a ladder can dictate what they're seeing without stopping work. A carer entering a facility can speak a quick observation note while walking.

title: Voice Notes vs Typed Notes: When to Use Each — Preserver Blog
text: A researcher in the field can narrate what they're photographing without putting the camera down. Voice is also better for nuance. Tone, emphasis, and context come through in a voice note in a way that a typed sentence can't always convey. If you're recounting a conversation, describing a complex scene, or summarising a meeting, speaking naturally produces a richer record than typing quickly. Hands are occupied or gloved You need to capture quickly — voice is faster than typing for most people The content is conversational or narrative You're in low light where typing is awkward You want to capture tone or inflection When typed notes win Text is better when the record will be searched, scanned, or shared. A typed note is immediately readable at a glance — in a list view, in an export, in a report. Voice notes require playback.

title: Voice Notes vs Typed Notes: When to Use Each — Preserver Blog
text: Text is also more precise for numbers, names, codes, or technical terms. Dictating "the serial number is BE-7-7-4-2-slash-Q" takes longer and is error-prone. Typing it takes three seconds. The content includes codes, numbers, or proper nouns You're in a quiet environment where speaking aloud would be awkward The note will be reviewed quickly without playback You need to record something brief and factual Combining both Nothing stops you from using both types in the same activity. A photo of a damaged component, followed by a typed note with the part number, followed by a voice summary of what happened — that's a complete record that covers different kinds of information efficiently. The best capture is the one you actually make. Use whichever method means you don't skip the record entirely. Both give you the same GPS and timestamp. Both are stored privately on your device.
